name: San Francisco waterfront flood defenses
aliases: San Francisco Waterfront Coastal Flood Study
SF Waterfront Flood Study Recommended Plan
acresNote: Not applicable: a 7.5-mile line of shoreline defenses along the Port of San Francisco's jurisdiction, from Aquatic Park to Heron's Head Park (Recommended Plan Highlights, Aug 2026, PDF pp. 9–10).

program.notes: Flood and seismic infrastructure; the housing and commercial fields don't apply. The USACE/City Recommended Plan combines floodproofing of piers and select buildings, raising and rebuilding wharves and historic buildings (including the Ferry Building and Ferry Plaza), raising the shoreline with seismically resilient structures, 2.8 miles of natural and nature-based features, two deployable closure structures and stormwater adaptations (Port staff report, Aug 7, 2026, PDF p. 5–6). First actions defend against 3.5 ft of sea level rise along the Embarcadero and 1.5 ft in South Beach/Mission Bay, adaptable later to as much as 7 ft (Highlights, PDF pp. 12, 24, 27). Estimated cost $17.8 billion in 2026 dollars ($14.1 billion design and construction, $3.7 billion real estate), at 20% design with a conditionally certified USACE estimate; if Congress approves, the federal government may pay up to 65% (staff report PDF p. 2; Aug 11, 2026 presentation PDF pp. 7, 14). The 2024 Draft Plan was estimated at $13.5 billion (2024 dollars). Separately, voters approved the $425 million Embarcadero Seawall Earthquake Safety Bond in 2018, and the City's capital plan schedules a $350 million Waterfront Safety & Climate bond for March 2028.

developer: Port of San Francisco (non-federal sponsor) with the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers
publicPartners: U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, San Francisco District
City and County of San Francisco (ClimateSF)
stageNote: Study complete, not authorized. USACE published the Final Integrated Feasibility Report and EIS on July 31, 2026, but there is no Record of Decision and no Chief's Report: the Chief of Engineers now requires 35% design before signing one, and the Port has been told it will not receive one on the 20%-design plan. Congress has not authorized or funded construction. The Port is designing early pieces with local money under a Section 221 agreement (Downtown Coastal Resilience Project, Broadway to Harrison; South Beach Coastal Resilience Project, Harrison to Townsend) and advocating for WRDA 2026 changes.

timeline.event: Congress approves a new start for the San Francisco Waterfront Coastal Flood Study with an initial $500,000 appropriation; voters approve the $425 million Embarcadero Seawall Earthquake Safety Bond.
USACE publishes its notice of intent to prepare an integrated feasibility report and EIS.
USACE and the City release the Draft Report and Draft Plan ($13.5 billion, 2024 dollars) for a 60-day comment period ending March 29.
Port Commission Resolution 24-62 authorizes a design and construction memorandum of understanding with USACE so the Port can advance design with local funds.
USACE's deputy commanding general confirms the Port will not receive a Chief's Report under the new 35% design rule.
The Port holds the first public workshop for the Downtown Coastal Resilience Project.
USACE publishes the Final Report and EIS with the Recommended Plan ($17.8 billion, 2026 dollars); the NEPA cooling period runs to Aug 31.
Port Commission hears an update on the Final Report, next steps and WRDA 2026 advocacy.

nextMilestone: Congressional action: Senate and House WRDA 2026 bills include provisions to expedite the study and (Senate) bar a blanket 35% design requirement; the Port has requested $10 million in FY 2027 Energy & Water appropriations to design the Downtown Coastal Resilience Project and planned to advertise northern and southern waterfront design contracts from August 2026.
summary: A plan to defend San Francisco's 7.5-mile Port waterfront, from Aquatic Park to Heron's Head Park, against sea level rise and earthquakes: raising the Embarcadero shoreline and seawall, rebuilding wharves and the Ferry Building's edge, levees and berms along Mission Bay and Islais Creek, and floodproofing elsewhere. The Army Corps' final study recommends it at $17.8 billion, but Congress has not authorized it; the first pieces near the Ferry Building and South Beach are in early design.
